speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm at Mabel Morris' house in Elk River today on the 26th of April. This is 1975 and we're going to ask Mrs. Morris some questions about what her life has been here in Elk River. You live here with your son and his wife.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They live with me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They live with you. This is your home.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This is my home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long have you lived here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This house was built in 1924. I came to Elk River in 1910.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you and your husband build this house? Yes. So it's your plan? Yes. All right, we'll start out with this personal data record. We'll just get this information and then we'll go into the other questions. Your full name is Mabel?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: M-A-B-E-L-L-E. M-A-B-E-L-L-E. Do you have that? M-A-B-E-L-L-E.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, Mabel. M-A-B-E-L-L-E. It's M-O-R-R-S.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: M-O-R-R-S.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: All right, and what was your maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Nicol. N-I-C-K-E-E-L-L.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: N-I-C-K-E-E-L-L. Have you ever had a nickname?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Every morning my little sister used to call me Bobo. I'd often wonder where she got it. She called me for years Bobo.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When were you born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, July 26, 1887.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where were you born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Rockwood, Ontario.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Rockwood? Uh-huh. What is your address here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just Elk River.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just Elk River, yes. Do you have a telephone number? Oh, I got that last night.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you get the right one? 3407.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 407, that's right. That's what you gave me last night. All right, when you first came to Idaho, you came directly to Elk River?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I worked in the post office in Potlatch.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you worked in Potlatch in the post office. And you came directly then from Ontario?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I lived in Duluth for a year before I came to Elk River.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And did you work there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I stayed in Elk River.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And so the year you arrived in Idaho was what year?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 1907. How did you travel? By train. Was there anyone with you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not with me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You came alone?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I came by myself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was your mother's maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A.P. Campbell. E.U.P.H.E.M.I.A. Her real name was Euphema Campbell.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: E-M-U-P-H-E-I-A-C-A-M-P-E-M. Do you know when she was born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I can't tell you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's all right. Then did she have any occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was just a post wife.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. Do you know where she was born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was born in D-O-R-N-O-C-H, Ontario.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: D-O-R-C-H, Ontario.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: D-O-R-N-O-C-H. Did you get it that way?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: D-O-R-N-O-C-H. What year did she die?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 1959. Do you know what year she was married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, but I can look it up and tell you. I've got the Bible in there that tells us when they were married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Maybe you'll have to read it later on then. Your father's name was what?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: John Robert Nickell.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was his occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was a farmer. Uh-huh. Do you know when he was born? Construction. He built bridges and one thing or another. I've got two. We did live on a farm. He lived on a farm and had men to look after it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. So he really had a profession other than farming. An engineer or a contractor?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I couldn't tell you what he had in those days because I don't know what they did have in there. But I know he was a construction man and he built bridges all over the country back there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Bridges mostly. And you know of? And you know of? Yes. Do you know when he was born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'd have to look it up. I'm not sure.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where was he born? Do you know that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Limehouse, Ontario.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And when did he die?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's another thing I'll have to look up because I just can't recall without looking it up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have brothers and sisters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had four sisters.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Can you tell me their first names?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Minnie E. Nickell was the woman. She's 90 now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, she's still living. Uh-huh. Did she marry? No. She still has Nickell.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was a dietician. She followed her profession until she was retired. And then... Kalina, she's the one that passed away. I don't know who you want. Do you want her? Yes. Kalina Rachel Nickell. She was a dietician also. She wasn't married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She's the one you traveled with for a while? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then I'm next. Uh-huh. You already got mine. Then there's Marjorie Frazier. Her name's Man now. She's married and lives up in Saskatchewan. And Margaret Ames. And she passed away... I can't tell you what they told me. There was an Easter, but what year was it? I don't know. Four years ago.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Aunt is right, deceased. Did you have brothers? No. No brothers?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: All right. And your husband's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: William George.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: William George. Uh-huh. When was he born? Do you know that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Hmm. December the 15th. I'm not sure of the date. I'd have to look it up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was his occupation? Durgast. Do you know where he was born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In Farmington, Iowa.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where were you married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In Spokane. The First Presbyterian Church in Spokane.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what date?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: December the 7th. December the 7th, 1909.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And when did your husband die?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Let's see, it was in 1946. October the 5th, 1946.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And let's see, talk about your children now. How many have you had? Just two. Two.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was this Chester Yangle?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Chester?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mrs. Chester Yangle. Yangle. Y-A-N-G-E-L.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Y-A-N-G-E-L.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They're down in Arizona for the winter. They ought to be home for the winter. G-E-A-L? Y-A-N-G-E-L.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just E-E-L. What was her last name? What was her first name? Lillian. Lillian. Where was she born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In Elk River.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Elk River. And when?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: January the 9th. 1912.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 1912. Has she had an occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She's a teacher.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She's a teacher. Is she still teaching? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She hasn't taught for some time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then your son is here. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: John? He's a druggist.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was. Was he born in Elk River? Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They were both born here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what was the date for him?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: May the 15th, 1918.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He's a druggist.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's a lieutenant colonel, too, in the Air Force.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Air Force Reserve. All right. How much education did you have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just high school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that was in Ontario? Yes. And you worked as a post...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In the post office.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Postmistress? Yes. And that was in Poplatch. Do you see yourself as having any other skills? Now, you do the sewing and quilting. Rug making. And you clerk in the drugstore.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've worked in the drugstore all my life. When it used to be a drugstore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's just a little bit of everything now.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: People don't know. Well, we had a hospital, you know, and a doctor here for years. And then when the mill went out, of course, they couldn't make a living here, so they had to move out.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How large was Elk River at its largest?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We had 1,200 people here at one time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 1,200 people, that's four times. Four times the size of...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We had a lot of beautiful homes here, and they moved them all out. In fact, there's one or two of the homes down in there in Moscow.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And there's one, just as you go down the Troy Hill, that, not two new ones, but the one on the other side is an Elk River house. And that one, just as you go into Deary, it's quite close to the road, that's an Elk River house too. They're all over the country down there, all kinds of them, several of them in Troy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it had to be a house in good, sturdy condition

speaker: Speaker 2
words: to be able to be moved. Of course, the potlatch built all the houses, and they all built up their own houses.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that how Elk River, when the mill came in, it was a mill town, and they built all the houses?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They built all the houses, in fact, they did all of them. Of course, anybody who wanted to build... No, we built this one ourselves, the potlatch didn't build it, we bought land and just built it, but most of the houses, the mill first started with all potlatch.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did people get it as part of their pay

speaker: Speaker 2
words: for working in the mill? No, no, they paid rent.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They paid rent.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They just built the houses and rented them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you want to tell me about any other skills that you have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I haven't got any more, I don't think. I always have my sewing. Sewing? I used to, when I was a little girl, I used to... Mother would buy material to make us dresses, and I'd snip a piece off to make a doll's dress. That's the way I learned to sew. She used to get awfully mad at me, too. A lot of times I got spanked.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just couldn't keep your hands off.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I used to cut up handkerchiefs, too, pretty handkerchiefs, and I'd snip it up and make a doll's dress out of it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Isn't that...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But Mother always said after I grew up, she said, well, that's the way I learned to sew. I make all my own clothes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Always have.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Always have made all my own clothes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When your children were growing up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Made them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you held any other jobs? No. Postmistress, and then after you married,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: you began working in the drugstore?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was your husband a druggist when you married him?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. He was a druggist in Potlatch.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's where you met him.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was in the drugstore in Potlatch. They had a huge store there, a big, big company store in Potlatch. And he worked in there. Came out from Iowa and had the job there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can keep an eye on this, so I make sure it's recording all the time. Do you have any other interests or hobbies? No. Well, you're a member of the Seringa Homemakers Club.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I've been with the club here a short while ago. Try to have something to do. Uh-huh. We used to have a bridge club, we used to have a five pounder club, but they don't play anymore at all. I don't know why.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So a bridge club. And what was the other one?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Five hundred club. Have you...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When your children were growing up, did you have... Did they have 4-H then or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not for... There's scouts. Mr. Morris had a scout troop.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you help with that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I didn't. He used to do it a little bit every old time. I never had time. I had to get up in the morning and grow it. I had a big garden. All this place back up here was in a garden. I had flowers. I had flowers all around the house.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you liked to grow flowers and vegetables.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'd get up at 4 o'clock in the morning and do that. Come in and do my housework, and then go to the store and work at 11 o'clock at night.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Quite a schedule.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We used to get the store open until 11.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What time would you open it in the morning?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sometimes we'd have to get up at 6 o'clock because they'd come to the house and want us. There was always somebody coming to the house and wanted us. Of course, we always went down when anybody wanted us. We generally tried to open up around 8.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You kept it open until 11. Long hours.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'd say they were long hours. People wonder. They say, oh, you've got lots of money. You earned it. I earned it, yeah. That's what I say. They worked out what we did, what I would do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you remember ever getting any special awards or ribbons or anything? Did you enter sewing in any way?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have a certificate from the president when I worked on the— when they were signing up the men for the war. I worked on all of those as a volunteer. I'd been on the election board for years and years and years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This was a certificate of appreciation.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I've got all of them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: For war, war award. And you worked on election boards.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I belonged to the Eastern Star and I belonged to the Rebecca's. I worked the maid room for the Eastern Star for three times. That was a lot of work, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Lodges and that kind of thing used to be more important than they are now. Yes, more people were—

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We don't have anything here anymore. All our lodges moved to Bougall. They did to Bougall and then they transferred to Durian in the wintertime. You see, they have vacation during the summer. And in the wintertime, the roads are not good enough. They get icy and mountainous, so we just don't go. I got my 50-year PIM for being—for the Eastern Star. And I've been a Rebecca for, put it another way, 55 years, I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Can you think of anything else you'd like to add to that list?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, if you do, we'll come back to it. All right. Do you—you talked some last night about the advantages of living in rural areas, what it is right now in general, as you look back over your whole life, would you by choice come to a rural area again?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I would. I don't like the city. I despise the city. I always have.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you were married how long?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, Mr. Morris died in 46. You were married in that time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We were married in 1909. So it would be the difference of—so he passed away.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You met him in Potlatch when you were working as a postmistress. He was a druggist there. Yeah. Okay. Would—I think it'd be interesting if you'd tell me now, start out from the time you were a child in Ontario, just a brief, so I get the sequence of your life.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there isn't too much that I can tell you. We lived on a farm. I had to walk over a mile to school, and I had— the other little odd thing I could tell you too about what we lived, we had a creek that went down to our farm. In fact, it bubbled up on the farm. It was ready to just bubble up, and it was ice cold all the time. We always had ice cold water. And my father dammed it up and built a milk house, and one way so it would churn the butter and make the butter. And he had crisscross things in there where we'd put milk, keep the milk in there to sort of keep cold. And it was all—there was all kinds of fish in it. And when they dammed it up, of course, there wasn't very much water down through the stream. And we'd go down there with pails. We always had a bunch of children up there. We had cousins in Toronto, and there'd be anywhere from maybe 15 to 18 or 20 children there during the summer just visiting. So we'd take pails and go down and get the fish and put them up in the pond above. And then, of course, we'd milk them. And they'd get all the milk out of them. They used to have more fun than they did. Outside of that, I think that's where we spent most of our time, when we were children. Because we always had a bunch of children there. The mother had two or three sisters, and they all had children. And then every one of those girls had friends, and we were always welcome to bring them home. We didn't bring them home any time we wanted to. So—but when I was little, that's the way we spent our time, down there in the creek. I told you all my parents, when they went there, I had arthritis, because my body was just ice cold and old.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you have some warm, happy memories of your childhood.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'll say we have.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you stayed there until you graduated from high school? Yes. How'd you happen to go to Duluth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had an uncle there. They had a daughter, and she died. And this uncle always said that I looked like the girl that he lost. And his mother let me come out for a visit. So I ended up there, and I stayed for a year. And in the meantime, I had another uncle come— he was living out here at Potlatch. He was the superintendent of the woods department. T.P. Jones, I don't know if you ever heard of him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, yes, I heard of him. He was your uncle.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And they were the ones that got me into the post office at Potlatch, because they lived out here. Aunt Marjorie, she was the only one around here, and so she wanted me to come with, so I came with. So that's how I landed on the woods.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you got the appointment as postmistress?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I just worked in there. My uncle, I had an uncle, Mr. Campbell, was the postmaster at that time, and I worked for him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And how long did you work then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, let me see. You know, in those days, where they used to— when the different parties, Republicans and Democrats, they changed the post offices every time. You remember that picture?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, when my uncle was a changed party, then everybody had been appointed by the—

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he lost the post office. Mr. McDonald, he wanted me to stay in there, and my aunt, she didn't want me to, so I went in with the cashier in the store for just a few months until I was married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This was the department store in Potlatch? How long did your courtship last? What was that like?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: About a year, I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you have dates? Would you entertain?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we used to welcome every night. So we boarded with the man that run the store. There was four of us that boarded with the man that run the store.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Both of you were in this house?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no, he wasn't. His folks lived up there. Mr. Morris' mother and father came out here. Mr. Morris was—he had charge of the furniture department in the store. And he always—he used to, when he had to send notes down in the little kid's, he used to put a note in and he'd tell me that his son was coming out, and I was just the right girl for him. He was always being—it was funny because he was scouting around for his son. Kind of a talented scout.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And so he had a pretty good idea what his son liked. Sure. That's interesting.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's why I happened to meet him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did clerking in a store involve in those days? Did you have to help?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I never did any clerking. I never was a clerk. I went right into the cashier's office.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you made change?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I'd make the change.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And kept track of sales?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I'd place note up in the ceiling and all these things come from all the different houses.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I remember seeing those things.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You used to put—the men used to put mice in and I used to live in horror. They'd send the snake up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, how—

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was playing tricks, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes. Well, I remember hearing somebody tell that that was before the time of adding machines. So you had to add everything up yourself. And that you could— Most women who worked like that became very expert.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I used to be able to add up to three or four hundred when I did. And just in my mind, I can't do it anymore. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But yes, that's what I heard about this woman. Became very expert just by having to do it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I used to add like that, too. Uh-huh. Sometimes now, if I'm feeling just right, I can do it. And down at the store, there's a place. I'm getting so now I can't see very good. My eyes are above that. That thing, I'm getting Cadillacs on my eyes. And it bothers me a little bit more. And I have to go down to the store. A lot of times, I'll add it up on the adding machine and I can't see it very good. Uh-huh. So I'll have to add it in my mind. Generally, I'm right. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's a good point, you know. You're limited by machines. Sure. So if you... I'll have to tell my son that when he keeps asking for a computer. I'll tell him it's better he'd learn to use his mind. That's more reliable in the long run. When you first got married, do you remember the reasons why you got married or just...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We just pretty much liked each other, I guess. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And nearly every woman got married at that time? But your sisters didn't, no.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they could have been married several different times, but they liked the work and they stayed with it, I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think they felt any put-downs or any lower status because they weren't married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So they're pretty...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: First of all, both traveled. Both of them have been around the world four or five different times. They'd just go in the winter and take a... go on board a ship and spend the winter.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's a pretty pleasant way to do it, isn't it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Some of the books that we were on a cruise with Adam on, they gave us these books about the ship that we were on. Oh, we did that. And this is the places that we visited on this one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, how exciting that would be. You got off the ship with these four.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and then we took trips. We had different trips. We went into Australia. We took a trip from Melbourne to Sydney and took in all the places that we wanted to visit. And we did the same in Japan when we were there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This was in 1957, you think? Yes. And you've seen all these pictures. Yes. And they've all changed a lot even since 1957.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I went over to Hawaii in... in... And that was right after the war practically. And everything was just as it was during the war. And when we went back the next time, Hawaii, I wouldn't have known it. They had to build all these skyscrapers in one day or another. It was just horrible. I didn't... I'm proud of that. I went back to Nevestan, Honolulu. That was an interesting place.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's something I've always wanted to see.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I enjoyed that very much. We went back two different times. We saw it in the morning. We saw it at noon. We got to see it at night. And it was different every time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, yes. I think I'd like to do that too if I were there. The Taj Mahal is just such a romantic... Was it everything you expected it to be?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was some more. Although there was a man here that had been over there during the war and he had a lot of pictures of it, so I had pretty good idea of what it would be like. But... I wasn't disappointed in any of it. I liked Japan. I thought that was... I liked India too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were those your two favorite places?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, at the time they were, but then when we went back the next time, we went to... I liked...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Africa.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I really enjoyed Africa.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What... I saw... Let's see, I saw East Africa here. Have you been in any other part? No. Here's the map that shows the... Oh, what is that thing? That is really some...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: experience.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You saw all these things?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that's... When we got off the ship, the ship gave us these books so we'd have something to know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Some background information.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okinawa, that was a lovely place. I enjoyed that. I got some beautiful pictures of the Diamond Head and sunsets from there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Like you say, now the skyline here is something else. Back to San Francisco.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then down to the... This is around Copacabana. You stayed there too? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that really was an experience. And how many... You've done this another time? Twice. Twice.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then this is one of the Japan-Pacific cruise. We were on that too. It was really lovely.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What a beautiful book.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that paper. Japanese.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That one, the paintings in there, they had an artist. They had... Oh, they gave dancing lessons and they gave painting lessons and they gave lessons on playing bridge and everything. They had people there and they... The days you were at sea weren't that bad at all. And the artist in there painted these pictures. I think there's some in there somewhere that they painted for the... That was interesting, Easter Island. Easter Island. Those peculiar heads.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they are...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They look just like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That I would like to see too. Polynesian Island. Those are very attractive pictures. I have a feeling you took advantage of everything they offered too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I did. Now these, she painted these. These were all hand-painted.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yes. That's the first one. She painted that one.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did they provide experiences for you to meet Japanese people and going to Hong Kong?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, we were entertained at the embassy in Canberra in Australia. We were entertained in the... in the... embassy in Japan. And what happened is that we knew Mr. Drew, the Canadian man from... He was over there as ambassador at the time. We knew him, so we were entertained there. That was special experience for you. When I was in England, we were at the Royal Garden Party at the Birmingham Palace. We had...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you saw Queen Elizabeth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, Queen Elizabeth and the prince and Margaret and her husband. And Princess Alice, I think it was. That was really an opportunity. I really feel like you're participating in something. Well, let's talk a little bit about Elk River now. What major changes have you seen?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Major things other than the...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't think I've seen anything good. Because we knew what... What had been proved because when we had the mill here, why, there was men who were working... In fact, Elk River had one of the biggest payroll in the Indian Empire when the mill was running. And of course, when the mill went out, everything was gone. The only thing we have here now is the men that works in the woods. And they ship most of the lumber out? Yeah, they ship it out by train. They haul it out by truck. So the profits go somewhere else. Ship. And they just kind of rob the land. Sure, that's right. The resources here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What's responsible for the change?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we built that big mill in Lewiston and everything goes down there now instead of the thing in Elk River. And they've been sorry ever since that they ever took the mill out of here because they said they were making more money on that here in Elk River. But a lot of the higher-ups didn't want to live in Elk River. They didn't want to live in the city. So they just got to talk them into moving the mill out. And when that mill... They took most of all the machinery out. And, you know, the oil, where they had oil, all the time there was oil every place. And then they decided to burn it down. And they set it on fire in the evening. And it was lit up just like day. And there was a plane that went over it, come over, and they cut the river, spook in. And of course John was in the Air Force and he knew how to... They kept flying over Elk River like it was trying to land. So he knew the signals and everything. So he went out and signaled. And they started out to go to Spook Dam. When they found out they were in the wrong place, they went down up here and around Wallace someplace. And they were burned up. Oh, how wonderful. And you could see clear up on top of the hill, every place, you could see just like daylight. That mill kept on churning fire. That seems like such a waste. Well, there wasn't anything left. They took most of the machinery out. Of course they wouldn't let them leave it there just to... So they burned it. That's what happened.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think you mentioned last night

speaker: Speaker 2
words: something about a big forest fire that took place. Yeah, that was in 1910.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Very shortly after the plane. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I've seen many forest fires. In fact, I've seen one come down here back at the school over here that got to go down to almost to the school when the wind changed into it all. Not that sure the whole town was gone. How did you make you and your husband

speaker: Speaker 1
words: decide to come to Elk River?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, the town was new and this man that ran it, when we first were married, when we first were married we went to Yakima and Mr. Morse worked for a man over there in Yakima. And when they started the mill, we knew Mr. Bloom, the superintendent, and he wanted us to come, he wanted Mr. Morse to come and start the drugstore. So we came. And we had two drugstores here at that time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right. And you were the last one there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We were the last one. The other ones only lasted... In fact, we were in this store that we're in now. We were in the other store. Did I show you the picture of the other building? This is the building we were in first, right here. Mr. Morse's father built this building. And this is the drugstore and this was Mr. Morse's brother and he had the hardware store. And we lived back here and his mother and father lived here and the other son that ran the hardware lived in this part. And this was in Elk River?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This was in Elk River. That was really an extensive family operation.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. And so we stayed here. And then these people, Mrs. Crawford from Bova, she had a drugstore down there and she came up here and built this brick building. And they only lasted about a year and a half or two years. And we brought them out.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So that's how we got... I think you heard something to say for the way you served the community. You were willing to get up when they needed something.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We worked too. We did. These fish, we used to come out... My uncle would come out here from Troquet and he was on business. He used wood soup and done in Troquet for the warehouser people. And he'd come out here on business and he called me up one day and he said, maybe I haven't got very much time, but he says, if you go out and get a mess of fish and make hot biscuits, he said I'll come up and have breakfast with you. So I told him, all right. We went out, Mr. Morse went out that morning and got a dishpan full of fish.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I had a platter full.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, the platter was this small, but the line was just heaped up. And he had another one of the warehousers with him. And he ate every one of them. And they'd have biscuits. That's all they had for breakfast.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And Mr. Morse would catch them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's all, one catch.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you catch them by hook or by arm?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: By hook and they were trouts. They were trouts.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you catch them one at a time or did you have a... No, no, no.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We caught them one at a time, but they just bite like everything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just as soon as you throw it in, they go and have it. That's fun. That's fun watching that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you can't let them go in and out of the fish tank. And in those days you didn't even have to have any kind of a certificate to go out and catch fish. You could go out and get all you wanted.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That bothers people now to have the government tell them when they can fish and when they can have...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's only a little bit conservative. They're conservative. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But it's hard getting used to that, isn't it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's where we lived until 1924. We had an apartment in the back.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then you got into the brick building.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I met.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: In the same year you built this house.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no, we were in the brick building before that. We were in the brick building about 1914, I think it was. We moved and bought that out. Because they only had it about a year before they had to sell it because they weren't making any money. She was losing money all the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, where did you live then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We still lived down there in the back of the building.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: In that same building? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We just moved the drugstore out. This is one of the stores that was down below there. And there's the Alcover. And there's the Alcover. These are all Alcover pictures.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Who walked by the drugstore walked down that direction and saw the old wooden sidewalks and traces of foundations of buildings. Yes. Who walked by the drugstore? The bar down there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That street that the drugstore was on, now there was a laundry on the far end. And there was a dentist, a Japanese dentist and a Japanese photographer. Had another building, two buildings here and there, and then there was a picture show. And then the hardware store and the bookstore were all in that block.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were they respected people in the community? Yes. And they've all gone.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There were a lot of Japanese people here at that time. A lot of Japanese that worked in the mill. Back to Almanover, when I was over in Japan, two of the boys came to see me that used to live here in Alcover. They came down and they were both in the U.S. Army. One of them was working in the post office department and the other one had two boys that lived here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, how nice. That really is. Do you know these people?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, this girl, she was in Yakima. The last I heard from her, she lived up here on that, you mean some of the streets? Her husband had bought that place up here on the hill. They had a lovely garden up there. They raised all kinds of things. Uh-huh. These people, when they moved out here, they had a grand piano and they had to carry it up. The only way they could get it up there to that building, there were no roads or anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was a world show, wasn't it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, the girls were quite talented. Their father was a millwright in the mill. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So, I think women in the past were pretty influential in bringing culture and that kind of thing to the community.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They both taught school. They both taught school here for quite a while.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So, they made kind of enhanced community life. Sure. And I understand some places they'd have community plays and programs put on.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There's the article about... This is the hospital that was here at the time, right here. That was up here on the hill above us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right up here? Yeah. Uh-huh. Oh, I'm glad you're pointing out these pictures to me. I can go back now and...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Here's the church.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We walked in there this morning. Susan told us that it was probably open and we walked in there. Those are beautiful glass windows. That took a lot of money.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The potlatch brought that church to the town. It was donated. And you know, children during the Depression, those mad children just took BB guns and broke all the windows out in the front.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I thought they replaced them with blue. Plain blue.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I was talking to someone the other day and I asked them about them and they said that they wasn't in the... They said they had taken the windows out of there and put other ones in. So, probably there's different windows in there. And they were going to try and see if they couldn't find out where they were made and get glass to fill them in. But there was a man in here, maybe six months ago, he was in there and asked me if I thought they'd sell those windows out of that church. And I said, sell them. I said, who gave you the idea they'd sell them? I said, nobody can sell those anyway because they're donated by the potlatch. And everybody's got the authority, but you know how they do now. They do anything to get a little bit of money.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That, you know, he just thinks he can come in and pay enough, he'd just walk away with whatever treasure he had in the community.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But those windows are there, they're real.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, they're beautiful. We walked in there and just sat and looked at them. What was the Depression like in Boulder? I mean, in Elk River?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we used to stay down there in the morning and close up in the afternoon and get in the car and go off to wherever we wanted to in the afternoon.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There just wasn't business.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There was no business. You couldn't buy anything. There was no money you could buy to sell. Mr. Morris went out here to Deep Creek and mine for wood. That's the way he spent his time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did he get enough to work his time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They paid their expenses, but they never made anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They gave them something to do. They weren't sitting around doing nothing, which is very damaging to people.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They built a business where they could, sushi, is that what they call it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have announced that they made it. It's real fine gold. Dust. Yeah, just the dust. I told John the other day, I said, I'm going to sell it for a hundred and some dollars.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's getting worth more all the time now, isn't it? I understand some of those might be worthwhile to open some of those mines again.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, please. We went over in Africa. We went to a mine over there where they were mining gold. We asked one of the cowboys or the people that worked there, that's when he said we did it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see, when your children were born, you had the hospital here and there were doctors here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we had a doctor here all the time. Up until 33, we had a doctor all the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you have any sense of not knowing how to raise your children? Your mother-in-law and father-in-law were here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I had two sister-in-laws.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So your children, you had a lot of adults there. Yes. And when you worked in the store, what did you do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, of course, when I worked in the store, I was living right back in the store there, and I knew where they were all the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you were in and out of your apartment and working, and it was just...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was home all the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the children ever come through the store? Did they help as they grew up, too?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, both of them worked in the store. John never said he wanted to. He didn't think that he'd like to work in the store.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But after he went to his war service, he came back?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He went to an air college back in St. Louis first. After he was out of high school, he had graduated when he was 16 from high school, and he didn't know what he wanted to do, but he wanted to go into the airplane work. So we sent him back to Parkes Air College in St. Louis, and he graduated from there. And of course, then the Depression come along, and he wanted to come home. Well, we didn't want him to come home because we didn't want him moving. When we told him he could come home, he would have to go to work or he had to come home and go to school. Either one or the other, he wasn't going to come home, just so. So he decided that he would go to school. So he went to school, and he started taking a condom. Mr. Marshall never said anything to him about studying to be a druggist or anything, because he didn't care if he did or not. He wanted him to do what he wanted to do. Come home one night and said he was going to be a druggist. So he graduated to be a druggist. I think he was running in oceans. I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many oceans has he done?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you know, I speak so much of the time, too. It's long hours. It's awfully long hours.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Still is. How long can you keep this door open now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. It's down there at about 11. He never gets home before 11 o'clock at night.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Five years long.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Too long.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about your daughter? How did she decide what she wanted to do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. She decided she was going to be a teacher.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did she go to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She went to Moscow part of the time, and then part of the time to Lewiston. She went to Lewiston for a while. And she taught here in Elk River most of the time when she taught.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And did she meet her husband yet?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Chuck worked for the potlatch. He hired a man for the company. And he was up here. He was living out here, and she met him here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He was kind of personnel director. Yes. Did they stay on then? Did she teach after she was married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She stayed in. In fact, they wanted to know yet. They call her all the time, but she doesn't do it anymore. She told us she couldn't call her. She has to drive back and forth to Bovo, and she didn't want to. They live over there. They live in Bovo, yes. For now. They're down in Arizona. They spend the winter in Arizona. They go down to Arizona every winter. They're down there now, but they're going to be home for a month.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is he retired now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, he's been retired for several years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, let's talk about your leisure time or recreation compared to when you were young and how it's changed through the years. Did you have time for any leisure time or recreation then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had a better time when the children were little. I did not.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because we had everything. We got on Monday, we did the washing. Tuesday, we did the ironing. Wednesday, we cleaned the house. Thursday, we did the boat. Friday, we did what we wanted to do. That was the system. You carried it out.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you got your work done and you had time for recreation.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We used to go visiting in the afternoon. We'd have a bunch of somebody say, what do you have for lunch and dinner today?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Come on over and bring what you got.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We'd go and there'd be a bunch of us. We'd spend the evening, maybe play cards or do anything we wanted to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it was a nice community.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sure. All the time. That's what we did. We'd do it on Sunday, on a Sunday afternoon. We'd have dinner and whatever we had left, we'd congregate at one of the houses. Everybody, probably, had a piano. I don't know why. We'd sing or just somebody would play and we'd sing hymns or on Sunday and have a good time in general.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just enjoy the game.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now you don't do that. Sure. Now you don't do any of that anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: People get in their cars and go someplace else. You go to see somebody, they leave the television on. Does that ever happen?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Lots of times. Does that bother you? Once in a while.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But people just don't go to see each other as often as they used to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, nobody goes anywhere anymore. We used to visit back and forth all the time. We had card parties. From the time I can remember that there wouldn't be a night. A lot of times there'd be an afternoon, but there wouldn't be something doing. My mother-in-law used to put on a program. We used to start up a program. We had beach clubs. We had another club that we had. We had the hostess would furnish the meat and the potatoes and the rest of the bunch would bring the rolls and the dessert and the salad and one thing or another and then we met every two weeks. From the time we had New Years until the first of April, whenever we had an evening, hardly there wasn't something doing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it wasn't an isolated dinner at all?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, it wasn't that isolated. I've had as many as eight tables for bringing in dinner many times.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. So...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was this when people had younger children? Did they bring the children and bring them down?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, they never brought them. They did have a babysitter.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They hired babysitters.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They never brought any of the children unless they were invited.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. What did you do in the summertime? Did you have big picnics?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We used to always go on a picnic. Go out and catch fish and fry them in the frying pan out there at Mountain Orchard. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Stay up there and spend the day. Uh-huh. Was this a Sunday activity or...?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mostly Sundays. Uh-huh. Up and down the roof, you see, in the daytime, they couldn't get away.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But this was the whole family went.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You know, everybody went.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's very pleasant.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We had a good time. Uh-huh. Nobody knew what times we had, really. And we had an awful nice bunch of people here because the student end of the mill, if we had anybody come in that wasn't desirable, they fired them right now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They were gone. And so they literally had to leave town.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they had to leave town because there wasn't anything for them to do here. So they kept the families that was here. They were all real nice people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. So they kind of regulated it that way. Sure.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever, um, when your husband was alive, did you ever worry about what might happen if he died or something happened to him?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I never did. He was always very healthy. He never seemed to, at any time, ever have been sick. And he evidently had a heart condition because I didn't know it. And I went east, my mother was there, and I went back east. And it was in November, he loved to hunt. Uh-huh. In fact, he just lived for his vacation to go hunting, and he liked to fish. And he went hunting, and he passed away just like that, just down in the woods. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, if he'd gone when you had the children young or anything, you would have had the store to make a living.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I would have had it. I could have run it too, as far as I could remember. I couldn't have been the drunk part of it, but the rest of it I could have. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You could have hired a driver.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I never even thought about it. I never even knew he was ill. He was all such a shock.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That didn't worry you at the time when the children were dependent on him?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. But they would go through school to see when it happened. Yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, when it actually happened. I guess what I was trying to get at was how would a woman make a living in those days if she had dependent children.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I guess they could do it. Uh-huh. Some would have had it, but they never would have grabbed these handles to get out.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. What would have—and it must have happened that sometimes men who worked for the lumber company were killed or injured.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they had no insurance.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that—

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If their husbands were killed in the woods, they got so much insurance, and then they lived on that until they remarried.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So if they could have stayed right here, they could live here. And they usually remarried.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A lot of them did. Uh-huh. We have a girl who lives here. She lost two husbands, so they both fell in the woods, and she got a pension until she remarried. And then, so she remarried, of course, the pension was taken away. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There was never ever any time then when you were the major support of your family? No. You worked before you were married, and did you support— you completely support yourself then? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see. You talked a little bit about your community and church activities you were involved in. You worked for the volunteer work during the war.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it was mostly Red Cross. I worked for them. I did all the cutting. I cut all the—everything that used to be sewed. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you organized the women?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I organized the women, but passed it out to whoever was supposed to do it. But that's what I did all the time during the war.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm. Was this both wars you did this? Mm-hmm. Both times? Yeah. When the Depression was on, did you increase the number of vegetables you grew with more support?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, because I always had a garden.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just always did. I always did have a garden, so it didn't mean so much that you didn't have money to go and buy food. You kind of supported your own stuff, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there was always plenty of my elbow. You know, you couldn't buy white flour. You couldn't get much sugar. But we could get honey, and I made oatmeal bread. Mm-hmm. And that was just as good as any other bread, as far as I could tell. Oh, yeah. It was like butter and cheese. Probably. Uh-huh. So we didn't suffer that way at all. We had our own vegetables.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There was just less business at the store. Well. And there was less money exchanged. Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's what I did. It was kind of different.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. So, um, what would, if you knew of a young woman that was starting out now to live like you did, what do you think she'd have to be able to do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think she would do anything. I don't think she'd know how to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You take the majority of these young girls now, and they go to the store and they buy canned stuff. They don't cook, and they don't do anything like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. You knew how to can your vegetables?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I can, and I made soups, and I made, in fact, I made everything. I made my bread and everything. Like, how many of them now do it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you know how to do this before you were married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I taught her. She knew how to do it. My mother taught all of us how to do it. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do. Uh, what magazines and newspapers do you read now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mostly the Geographic. I get the AARP magazine, and I get the Arizona Highways, and I get Sunset. Do you have television?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have a favorite program?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I like the Daltons, and I like Lawrence Welk, and, um, oh, I watch quite a few of the different shows that they have on. There isn't really anything I particularly crazy about. I watch, uh, As the Wheel Turns.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh, uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We had that on the Weekend Lunch, and, well, we watched that one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you're busy all morning.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You work every morning in the dorms. I go down and help with the cook the meal comes in the morning. That's when I have my shift. The afternoons are early. I ain't got nothing doing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh, so people come in to check their mail, and they take care of it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they come in, give them what they want, and then they go home and stay. Uh-huh, uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So that's kind of a pattern in this.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, shut the door? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you were running the business, and your husband was alive in the store, did you help make decisions about the store?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Or was that his business?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we just worked together. I never really...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was now a working-interest in itself.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, uh-uh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: One person's job or another person's job, which is kind of...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We always had help. We always had a girl in there, too. Uh-huh. A lot of times I stayed at home. I didn't go down. If I had something to do at home, I generally... I'm home to do it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever have help with the housework?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've always had help, always. I've had help ever since I was married. I never done any of the washing or anything like that. Could rub the wash on the board. Was it one of the older...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Teenage girls or...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I had another one that worked for me. She knew this.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I see.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She'd come and she'd do the washing. A lot of times if I was busy, she'd come in and do the ironing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was she a widow or...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was a widow.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. That was a thing that they usually did. Um... The decision to come here, was this both your husband and you made that decision? Yes. And it just worked out.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Um...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Has there ever been a time when you've had strong feelings about how much you like being a woman or you dislike being a woman? Can you identify any? Uh-uh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It just...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Met your problems and enjoyed life? Too much.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. Uh-huh. There were many a reason to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I never...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anything else now? I've asked you a lot of questions. Have you... Any other things you'd like to tell me about your life

speaker: Speaker 2
words: as you look over it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you have changed anything if you could have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think so. I was thinking about that the other day. I wouldn't change anything. You know, there's no use in worrying about things like that. You have to take it as it comes. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was marriage about what you expected it to be? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have a wonderful husband. He's a very wonderful person. May I have a picture of him over there, do you want to see?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, I'd like to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This is an obvious picture of him because he was taken from another picture. You can never be sure of something.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yes. Looks like a solid citizen in the community. He was.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mr. Martin is very well thought of. He was a... Everybody say he was a wonderful person. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm sure he was a leader in the community and helped make decisions for us.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And what was his origin?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Named after him, he was a mountain named after him. Well, that's pretty good, isn't it? Uh-huh. So people know he was in the community. Yes. He left a part. You know, must have been a great shock to have to lose him.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'll say. And so sudden, too. I was in the east when it happened. I was going to tell the family thing and come home, but he had passed away and I was it. Uh-huh. That's...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's very hard, yet I think other times when people have long, lingering deaths, sometimes that's not very good.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Can we just get him to the back of the chair? And I'm almost through.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of the biggest problems you met in trying to readjust to living without him?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think I had any because I worked all the time. I went right back to work in the store and I was kept busy all the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So that's important.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And it's the only thing you can do because there isn't anything to sit at home and worry about.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There's no more things that can be helped. Uh-huh. Did you ever consider remarrying? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Never even thought about it. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was there a difference in your social relationships after that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, considerably, because we're all friends that we went out with. I figure all the husbands are still alive and when you're alone like that, it makes a big difference.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. So you literally had to find new friends, other women who were single.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, about that time that practically everybody left Elk River, there was lots of them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: About the same time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, all my friends that was here during those days are all living in Spokane, some of them in Moscow, Mizunarino, and a lot of them in Moscow that has lived here in Elk River. Sure. You know, you just gradually... As far as the younger people here, I like them and everything, but I don't really want to be with them because they don't have anything in common with what I have. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have a few friends your age?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, here in town? Yes. There's nobody here. Mrs. Vines is the only one that's left. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you joined the Tseringa Homemakers group, but they still aren't exactly...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, they're not people that I've been in with at all. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you write letters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Lots of letters. Lots of letters. I have a lot of friends in California, I've got a lot of friends in Spokane. Uh-huh. So I guess... I mean, I have all kinds of friends up in Canada that I still write to that I've had during the years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you anticipate getting to travel to visit them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm considering going back now because the sister in Moscow's estate is being settled up, and her other sister that she lives with is 90 years of age, and she wants to stay in the house by herself, and she's getting quite forgetful, she's getting thrown out, and she doesn't remember from when to the next what she's done. So we just insist that she's got to give up the house, and go into an apartment and come out here with us, and she doesn't want to come out here with me because all her money is in Canada, and it makes a difference, you know, to have to change congressmen. So we don't know what we're going to do, and so I think possibly in about two or three more weeks that I'll be going east, and see what's going to happen back there. I wrote her a letter the other day and told her that she just had to give it up to them, and she said, well, what will I do with all the furniture? And I said, well, you just have to sell it. Take what she needs for her apartment and let the rest of it go. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. So everything's up there. There isn't anything settled yet or anything, so we don't know what to do. And of course, they wanted me to come back when my sister passed away, but just about that time I had a heart condition. I couldn't travel very well because I couldn't walk. And so I didn't go back. It's a good job I didn't because I'd have been probably back there when Bill passed away.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This was your grandson? Uh-huh. That's been pretty recent, isn't it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Two days, the 31st of January. Uh-huh. That was a shock. That was a terrible shock. Because they come home every weekend, and he always was. He was a kid who liked home. Uh-huh. And just to have him take the night path.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many grandchildren do you have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just the two. John's the only one who has two. Lillian has many children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So this is the—and this little baby is Bill's baby. That's Bill.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Bill. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The mother, her sister is having the baby. They called this little wife and said she had a 7 1⁄2 pound boy. Oh, so you just got the news. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, did she want a boy?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She wanted a boy, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So she's really happy now.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. So we're—Jandalee's got a cousin.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. Well, that's very—that's Jandalee that's here. Uh-huh. Well, unless you would like to add something that I haven't asked you about.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think I heard it pretty well. I think—well, this is what we call the release form. And I don't know that I explained it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You said with her that you planned to have a pit. You know, you always did. He never got a piece of pie. Nobody got a pit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Nobody got a pit.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You remember that. Yes. He used to get it all the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think the way she talks about her experiences in the dining room

speaker: Speaker 2
words: and she just enjoyed being with people, you know,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: and had so many contacts. I think she really remembers that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She used to come in and ask him if he'd thrown the pit, and he'd say, no, not yet. I often told him, I said, I think you carry it around in your pocket. Traveller.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's real.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's real. But I wasn't going to say we went up to Marano's there,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: but they were moving down there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And here we were, one of the seaters. We went down to the funeral. We didn't have to wait here. And we went up to see how Bill was. He's had a stroke, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She mentioned something about that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's done a bit well, and I just wondered if you'd seen him lately.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I haven't. I heard her mention something about he fails so much.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Part of the time, he loved Elk Grove. He used to work in the printing office here. He owned the printing office here for a while, during when the mill was here. And while we were there, he was in Elk River. He thought he was living in Elk River. And then Sophie told me that she says that's where he wants to go. He wants to go to Elk River all the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was his happiest time of life.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And he kept asking. She said, well, as soon as the snow is gone, we'll go to Elk River. They usually come up once or twice during the summer months to spend a little bit of time. But he can't, she said he can't drive anymore. And Sophie, I guess, didn't drive very much. She'd drive around town. She said his brother was coming over from, I don't know if he lives in Portland, he lives over on the coast somewhere. She said when they came over, they'd bring him up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, it's really been an experience the short time I've been here. And I look forward to coming back. Now I even know more about the community. I hope that we'll come back any time. Thank you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Come up and see me. Thank you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Thank you. Would you sign these here then, and I'll tear them in half. This one here and this one here. Yes, so it says signature and signature. Certainly they wouldn't have farm chores and things like that, of course. No.
